title: Google Analytics 4
tagline: Measure a website the way GA4 does, and turn the numbers into decisions, with live reports and SQL
summary: Learn how Google Analytics 4 thinks: events, parameters and users, how data is collected with the tag and Google Tag Manager, how traffic is grouped into channels, and how to read acquisition, engagement and conversion. You build the reports yourself, live in your browser, on the sessions of a small learning site: rates, trends, heat maps and funnels, plus SQL on the same traffic as flat events, the way GA4 data looks in a BigQuery export. The GA4 interface, Google Tag Manager and BigQuery themselves are explained and shown as listings; they need a Google account and a real site, so they do not run here.

modules.title: Web analytics and the GA4 data model
modules.summary: Understand what web analytics is for, how GA4 records everything as events, and how users, sessions, dimensions and metrics fit together.
modules.outcome: You can say what questions analytics answers, describe GA4's event-based model, tell a dimension from a metric, and define users, sessions, engaged sessions and engagement rate.
modules.intro: Every website and app owner asks the same questions: who comes, where from, what do they do, and does it lead to something we want? Google Analytics 4 (GA4) answers them by recording what visitors do as a stream of events and turning those events into reports. Used well, it shows where marketing works and where the site loses people; used badly, it produces confident numbers that mean nothing. This course teaches the model and the judgement. Google Analytics itself is a cloud service that needs your own website and Google account, so you cannot open it inside this course. What does run here: a practice report builder (dimensions, metrics, calculated metrics, filters and charts, like GA4's Reports and Explorations) on the traffic of a small learning site, and a SQL window on that traffic as it appears in a GA4 export. The lessons describe the real GA4 screens and settings as of this writing; Google changes the interface and some names often, so always check the current help pages.

topics.title: What web analytics is for
topics.html:
Web analytics measures behaviour on a website or app so people can decide what to improve. The value is in the questions, not the tool.

Questions analytics answers
AreaTypical questionExample decision
AcquisitionWhere do visitors come from?Shift budget to the channel that brings buyers
BehaviourWhat do they do on the site?Rewrite a page people leave at once
ConversionDo they do what we want (buy, sign up, enquire)?Fix the step of checkout where most people drop out
AudienceWho are they (device, country, new or returning)?Make the mobile experience work, because most visitors are on phones
RetentionDo they come back?Send a reminder email to people who did not finish
Worked example

From a number to a decision

A learning site sees 12,000 visits in a month.

  1. The number alone says nothing: is that good?
  2. Split it: 55% of visits are on mobile, but mobile visitors rarely buy.
  3. Decision: test a simpler checkout on phones, then compare the mobile conversion rate next month.

Answer. Analytics is useful when a measure points to a change you can test.

Watch out

Vanity metrics (total visits, page views, followers) feel good but do not tell you whether the business is better off. Prefer measures tied to goals: sign-ups, purchases, revenue, return visits.

Common mistakes

  • Collecting everything and asking no questions.
  • Reporting visits as success without conversions.
  • Changing the site and not measuring the effect.
Try it yourself: Which is a better success measure for a course website: total page views or enrolments?

Model answer. Enrolments: they are tied to the goal. Page views can rise while enrolments fall.

Check what you just learned

1. A vanity metric is one that:
  • Always matters most
  • Is always zero
  • Is hidden
  • Looks good but does not show whether goals are met (correct)

Prefer outcome measures.

2. The best starting point for analytics is:
  • A goal and the questions it raises (correct)
  • Installing every tag
  • A colour scheme
  • A bigger server

Questions come before data.
keyPoints: Analytics answers questions about acquisition, behaviour, conversion, audience and retention.
Start from goals; prefer measures tied to outcomes over vanity metrics.
Analytics works as a loop: measure, learn, change, measure again.

topics.title: The GA4 data model: events, parameters, users and sessions
topics.html:
GA4 is event-based: every interaction is recorded as an event with a name and extra detail called parameters. A page view is an event. A scroll is an event. A purchase is an event. Reports are built by counting and grouping events.

The building blocks
ConceptMeaningExample
EventSomething a user didpage_view, scroll, purchase
Event parameterDetail about an eventpage_location, value and currency on a purchase
User propertyA fact about the user that persistsA plan type or a language
SessionA group of events from one visit; starts with a session_start eventA visitor browsing for 8 minutes
UserA person (or browser or device) identified by an identifierCounted as 'users'
Data streamA source of data sent to GA4 (a website or an app)Your website's web stream, with a measurement id like G-XXXXXXXXXX

The hierarchy in the product is Account → Property → Data stream. An account holds properties (usually one per business or site), and a property holds streams for each website or app.

What changed from Universal Analytics
Universal Analytics (the old version)GA4
ModelSessions and hit types (page views, events)Everything is an event
SessionsCore unit of reportingDerived from events (session_start)
Apps and webSeparateOne property can combine web and app streams
Bounce rateCentral metricReplaced mainly by engagement rate
StatusStandard Universal Analytics properties stopped processing new data in July 2023The current product
Worked example

Reading a purchase as events

A visitor lands on a product page and buys.

  1. session_start, then page_view (the landing page).
  2. view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout.
  3. purchase with the parameters value, currency and the items bought.

Answer. The whole journey is a short list of events; a funnel is just counting how many sessions reach each one.

Watch out

GA4 data is not instant or perfect. Standard reports can take hours to complete, numbers differ from other tools (for example server logs or a payment system), and consent choices and ad blockers hide some visitors. Treat GA4 as a good estimate of behaviour, not an exact ledger.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting GA4's totals to match the payment system exactly.
  • Thinking a 'user' is always one person: it is usually a browser or device.
  • Comparing Universal Analytics history directly with GA4: definitions differ.
Try it yourself: What does GA4 record when someone scrolls down a page?

Model answer. An event (scroll, when enhanced measurement is on) with parameters such as the page location.

Check what you just learned

1. In GA4 a page view is:
  • A hit type only
  • An event (correct)
  • A property
  • A report

Everything is an event.

2. A session starts with:
  • A purchase
  • A report
  • A session_start event (correct)
  • A cookie banner

GA4 creates a session_start event.
keyPoints: GA4 records every interaction as an event with parameters.
Sessions and users are derived; the hierarchy is account, property, data stream.
Numbers are estimates; they will not match other systems exactly.

topics.title: Dimensions and metrics: users, sessions and engagement
topics.html:
Every GA4 report is dimensions (what you break the data down by) and metrics (the numbers). It is the same idea as Tableau's or SQL's: dimensions group, metrics count.

Common dimensions and metrics
Examples
DimensionsDate, Session default channel group, Session source / medium, Device category, Country, Landing page, Page path, Event name
MetricsUsers, New users, Sessions, Engaged sessions, Engagement rate, Average engagement time, Event count, Key events, Total revenue
Definition

Engaged session. A session that lasted at least 10 seconds, or had at least one key event, or had at least two page or screen views. Engagement rate is engaged sessions divided by sessions. Bounce rate in GA4 is the opposite: sessions that were not engaged, divided by sessions.

Formula · Engagement rate

engagement rate = engaged sessions ÷ sessions

A rate of 0.62 means 62% of sessions were engaged. Always compare rates at the same level (by channel, by device), not as an average of averages.

Build a report: sessions by channel

Sessions and Users are ready-made metrics. Put Channel on Columns and Sessions on Rows. Then try Device, Country or Landing Page, and swap in Users.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Session ID, User ID, Session Date, Channel, Source / Medium, Device, Country, Landing Page, Engaged, Engagement Seconds, Pageviews, Converted, Revenue.

The metric Users needs care. GA4's reports show Active users by default: people who had an engaged session or the first-visit event. Total users counts everyone who triggered any event. The two differ, so say which you mean.

Worked example

Sessions are not users

A learner visits on Monday and again on Wednesday.

  1. Users: 1 (the same person).
  2. Sessions: 2 (two separate visits).
  3. A user with many sessions is a returning user, usually your most valuable audience.

Answer. Always check whether a number counts people or visits.

Watch out

Metrics can be misread across dimensions. Users are not additive: a person who visits on mobile and on desktop is counted once in total but once in each device row, so the device rows add up to more than the total. Never add up user counts across rows.

Common mistakes

  • Adding user counts across channels or devices.
  • Mixing up sessions and users.
  • Quoting an engagement rate without saying what was in the denominator.
Try it yourself: What makes a session 'engaged' in GA4?

Model answer. It lasted at least 10 seconds, had a key event, or had two or more page or screen views.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a dimension?
  • Sessions
  • Key events
  • Engagement rate
  • Device category (correct)

It breaks the data down.

2. Engagement rate is:
  • Engaged sessions ÷ sessions (correct)
  • Users ÷ sessions
  • Events ÷ users
  • Revenue ÷ users

Share of sessions that were engaged.
keyPoints: Dimensions group data; metrics are the numbers.
Engagement rate = engaged sessions ÷ sessions; bounce rate is the opposite.
Users are not additive across rows; sessions and users are different things.

topics.title: A tour of GA4's reports and where numbers come from
topics.html:
GA4's interface has a handful of areas. Knowing what each is for saves a lot of searching.

The main areas
AreaWhat it is for
HomeA quick overview and shortcuts
ReportsStandard, ready-made reports: Reports snapshot, Realtime, Acquisition, Engagement, Monetization, Retention, and User attributes and Tech
ExploreExplorations: build your own analyses (free-form tables, funnels, paths, cohorts)
AdvertisingAttribution and conversion paths across channels
AdminSettings: data streams, events, key events, data retention, users and permissions, links to other products

Habits when reading a report

  • Check the date range and the comparison (previous period or year).
  • Check the property and filters: internal traffic excluded?
  • Look at the dimension you are viewing by, and what segment or filter is applied.
  • Be careful with the latest day or two: data may still be arriving.
  • Ask what the number is a share of (sessions, users, events).
Worked example

A report that misleads

The Acquisition report shows Direct as the largest channel.

  1. Direct often includes visits GA4 could not attribute (a missing campaign tag, a link in a messaging app).
  2. If your emails are untagged, their visits fall into Direct.
  3. The honest reading: 'Direct includes unattributed traffic', and fix the tagging.

Answer. Large 'Direct' numbers are often a tagging problem, not loyal visitors.

Watch out

Google Analytics itself is a cloud service that needs your own website and Google account, so you cannot open it inside this course. What does run here: a practice report builder (dimensions, metrics, calculated metrics, filters and charts, like GA4's Reports and Explorations) on the traffic of a small learning site, and a SQL window on that traffic as it appears in a GA4 export. The lessons describe the real GA4 screens and settings as of this writing; Google changes the interface and some names often, so always check the current help pages.

Common mistakes

  • Reading the newest day as final.
  • Treating Direct as only people who typed your address.
  • Comparing periods of different length.
Try it yourself: Where would you build a custom funnel analysis in GA4?

Model answer. In Explore (an Exploration), using the Funnel exploration.

Check what you just learned

1. Custom analyses such as funnels are built in:
  • Home
  • Explore (correct)
  • Admin only
  • Realtime

Explorations are the build-your-own area.

2. A very large Direct channel often means:
  • Loyal customers only
  • No traffic
  • Unattributed traffic, often from missing tags (correct)
  • Bots only

Check campaign tagging.

Key terms: flip and sort

Event
Something a user did, recorded with parameters.
Parameter
Detail attached to an event.
Session
A group of events from one visit.
Dimension
What you break data down by.
Metric
A number such as sessions or revenue.
Engaged session
10 seconds, a key event, or two page views.
Data stream
A website or app sending data to a property.
keyPoints: Reports are ready-made; Explore builds custom analyses; Admin holds settings.
Check dates, comparisons, filters and what a number is a share of.
Large 'Direct' often means unattributed traffic.

modules.title: Collecting good data: events, tags and campaigns
modules.summary: Choose and name events, send them with a tag and a data layer, tag campaigns with UTM parameters, and keep the data clean and consent-aware.
modules.outcome: You can tell automatic, enhanced, recommended and custom events apart, describe how Google Tag Manager's tags, triggers, variables and data layer work, tag campaigns correctly, and list the settings and checks that keep data trustworthy.
modules.intro: Reports are only as good as the data behind them, and the data is only as good as the tagging. Missing campaign tags push traffic into Direct; a misnamed event splits one action into three; a test visit by your own team inflates sessions. This module is about getting the collection right: which events to track, how a tag sends them, how to tag campaigns, and how to check and protect the data. Google Analytics itself is a cloud service that needs your own website and Google account, so you cannot open it inside this course. What does run here: a practice report builder (dimensions, metrics, calculated metrics, filters and charts, like GA4's Reports and Explorations) on the traffic of a small learning site, and a SQL window on that traffic as it appears in a GA4 export. The lessons describe the real GA4 screens and settings as of this writing; Google changes the interface and some names often, so always check the current help pages.

topics.title: Events: automatic, enhanced, recommended and custom
topics.html:
GA4 gives you four kinds of events, from least to most work.

Event types
TypeWhat it isExamples
Automatically collectedSent as soon as the tag is installedfirst_visit, session_start, user_engagement
Enhanced measurementOptional events you switch on in the data stream settingspage_view, scroll, outbound click, file_download, site search, video engagement, form interactions
RecommendedEvents Google has defined names and parameters for, which you implementlogin, sign_up, generate_lead, and the ecommerce events view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase
CustomEvents you invent for your own needsbrochure_download, calculator_used

Count events and sessions

Seventeen events from five sessions. COUNT(*) counts events; COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) counts sessions. Which event do all sessions have?

Tables: ga_events. Starting query:

SELECT event_name,
       COUNT(*) AS events,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
FROM ga_events
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY sessions DESC, event_name;

Naming and design rules

  • Use recommended events and their names where one exists: GA4's reports and integrations understand them.
  • Name custom events in lowercase with underscores (brochure_download), and keep names consistent.
  • One event for one action, with parameters for the detail (item_name, link_url), not a new event per detail.
  • Do not put personal data (names, emails, phone numbers) in event names or parameters.
  • Mind the limits: event names and parameter counts are limited, and custom dimensions must be registered before they appear in reports.
  • Document every event in a tracking plan.
Worked example

One event, not three

A site tracks downloads of three brochures.

  1. Poor: events download_brochure_a, download_brochure_b, download_brochure_c.
  2. Better: one event brochure_download with a parameter brochure_name.
  3. Now you can report downloads in total and by brochure, and adding a fourth brochure needs no change.

Answer. Events name the action; parameters carry the detail.

Watch out

Parameters you send are not available in reports automatically. To use a custom parameter in a report or an exploration you register it as a custom dimension or metric in Admin, and it only collects from then on, not backwards.

Common mistakes

  • A new event name for every variant of one action.
  • Personal data in parameters.
  • Sending a parameter and never registering it.
Try it yourself: Which type of event is purchase?

Model answer. A recommended event (one of the ecommerce events Google defines).

Check what you just learned

1. Which is an enhanced measurement event?
  • purchase
  • login
  • brochure_download
  • scroll (correct)

Scroll tracking is an enhanced measurement option.

2. Custom parameters appear in reports after you:
  • Register them as custom dimensions or metrics (correct)
  • Do nothing
  • Rename the site
  • Restart GA4

Registration is required, and is not retroactive.
keyPoints: Events are automatic, enhanced, recommended or custom; use recommended names where they exist.
One event per action, with parameters for the detail; no personal data.
Register custom parameters as custom dimensions or metrics to use them in reports.

topics.title: Tags, triggers and the data layer
topics.html:
A tag is a small piece of code on your site that sends data. You can add the Google tag directly, but most teams use Google Tag Manager (GTM): a container on the site where marketers manage tags without editing the website's code each time.

GTM's building blocks
PieceMeaningExample
TagWhat to send and whereA GA4 event tag that sends brochure_download
TriggerWhen to send itA click on a link ending in .pdf
VariableA value a tag or trigger can useThe clicked link's URL, or a value from the data layer
Data layerA structured object the site fills with information for GTM to readThe order total and items at checkout
ContainerThe package of all tags, triggers and variablesOne container per site

Working safely with tags

  • Use Preview mode in GTM and DebugView in GA4 to watch events arrive before publishing.
  • Work in a workspace and publish versions with notes, so a change can be rolled back.
  • Give tags, triggers and variables clear names (GA4 - brochure_download).
  • Keep the data layer's names stable: the site team and the analytics team must agree on them.
  • Restrict who can publish: a wrong tag can break the site or collect personal data.
Worked example

Debugging a missing event

Purchases are not appearing in GA4.

  1. In GTM Preview, confirm the data layer push happened and the trigger fired.
  2. If the tag did not fire, check the trigger's conditions (a typo in the event name).
  3. If it fired, open DebugView and check the event arrives with its parameters.

Answer. Test each link in the chain: site, data layer, trigger, tag, GA4.

Watch out

Tags can collect personal data by accident: a form field's text, an email in a URL, a name in a parameter. Review what each tag sends, and keep personal data out of GA4.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing changes without Preview.
  • Many people with publish rights and no change notes.
  • Hard-coding the tracking in the page and again in GTM, so events are counted twice.
Try it yourself: What is the data layer for?

Model answer. A structured place where the site puts information (such as a purchase's value and items) for the tag manager to read and send.

Check what you just learned

1. A trigger decides:
  • What to send
  • When a tag fires (correct)
  • Which colour to use
  • Who can see the report

It is the condition for firing.

2. The data layer is:
  • A report
  • A password
  • A structured object the site fills for GTM to read (correct)
  • A chart

It carries values from the site to GTM.
keyPoints: GTM manages tags, triggers and variables in a container; the data layer carries structured information from the site.
Test with Preview and DebugView before publishing; use versions and clear names.
Review what tags send to avoid collecting personal data.

topics.title: Campaign tagging: UTM parameters and channels
topics.html:
GA4 learns where a visit came from from the referrer and from UTM parameters you add to the links of your campaigns. Without them, much of your marketing traffic lands in Direct.

The UTM parameters
ParameterMeaningExample
utm_sourceWhere the link was placednewsletter, instagram
utm_mediumThe type of channelemail, cpc, social
utm_campaignThe campaign namespring_sale_2025
utm_termA paid search keyword (optional)sql course
utm_contentWhich version of an ad or link (optional)blue_button

GA4 groups traffic into default channel groups using rules on source and medium: for example a medium of email gives Email, cpc or ppc gives Paid Search (when the source is a search engine), organic from a search engine gives Organic Search, social gives Organic Social, and no source at all is Direct.

Source / medium to channel
Source / mediumDefault channel group
google / organicOrganic Search
google / cpcPaid Search
newsletter / emailEmail
instagram / socialOrganic Social
partner-blog.in / referralReferral
(direct) / (none)Direct

Tagging discipline

  • Agree naming conventions: all lowercase, no spaces, consistent source and medium names.
  • Never tag internal links on your own site with UTMs: it starts a new session and hides the real source.
  • Use a shared spreadsheet or builder so everyone tags the same way.
  • Tag every campaign link: emails, ads, social posts, QR codes, partner links.
  • Do not put personal data in UTM values: URLs are stored and shared.
Worked example

A broken tag

An email link uses utm_medium=Email in one campaign and utm_medium=e-mail in another.

  1. GA4 treats Email, email and e-mail as different values.
  2. e-mail may not match the Email channel rule, so those visits land in Unassigned.
  3. Fix the convention and re-tag future links.

Answer. Inconsistent tags fragment channels; consistent lowercase names keep them whole.

Watch out

UTM values are case sensitive in reports: Newsletter and newsletter are two sources. Choose one style, such as all lowercase, and stick to it.

Common mistakes

  • Tagging internal links.
  • Mixed capital letters and spellings.
  • Leaving paid links untagged and relying on auto-tagging alone without checking the link between ad and analytics accounts.
Try it yourself: Which medium would an email newsletter link use?

Model answer. email (so GA4 groups it as the Email channel).

Check what you just learned

1. A medium of `email` groups traffic as:
  • Paid Search
  • Referral
  • Direct
  • Email (correct)

The Email channel rule.

2. Why avoid tagging internal links?
  • It starts a new session and hides the real source (correct)
  • It is slow
  • It deletes data
  • It is illegal

Internal UTMs overwrite the source.
keyPoints: UTM parameters tell GA4 the source, medium and campaign of a link.
Default channel groups are assigned from source and medium; consistent lowercase naming keeps channels clean.
Tag every campaign link, never internal links, and keep personal data out.

topics.title: Data quality, consent and privacy basics
topics.html:
Collecting data responsibly means it is clean and lawful.

Keeping data clean
ProblemFix
Your own team's visits inflate sessionsDefine internal traffic (IP addresses) and activate the internal traffic data filter
Payment or login sites appear as referrals and break sessionsAdd them to the unwanted referrals list
Duplicate events (a hard-coded tag and a GTM tag)Keep one implementation; test in DebugView
Bots and spamGA4 filters known bots automatically; watch for unusual spikes
Cross-domain journeys split into two usersConfigure cross-domain measurement
Test data in the production propertyUse a separate test property or filter test traffic

Consent and privacy

  • Many laws (such as the EU's GDPR and India's DPDP Act, 2023) set rules on consent and personal data; the details depend on where you and your visitors are.
  • A consent banner asks visitors' permission before analytics or advertising cookies are set.
  • Consent Mode lets Google tags adjust their behaviour based on the visitor's consent choices, so a visitor who declines is not tracked in the usual way.
  • GA4 does not store full IP addresses, and offers data retention settings (for example 2 or 14 months for user-level event data) and controls for data deletion.
  • Do not send personal data to GA4 (names, emails, phone numbers), and do not rely on tools to anonymise it later.
Worked example

Why the numbers drop after a banner

A site adds a consent banner and sees traffic in reports fall 30%.

  1. Visitors who decline analytics are no longer measured in the usual way.
  2. Reports now undercount real visits; trends before and after are not comparable.
  3. Note the change on a timeline annotation and compare like with like.

Answer. Lawful collection can reduce your measured numbers. That is expected: record when it happened.

Watch out

This is general information, not legal advice. Ask your organisation's privacy or legal team what consent and retention rules apply to your site and audience.

Common mistakes

  • No internal traffic filter.
  • Collecting data before consent where consent is required.
  • Treating a drop after a consent change as a real fall in demand.
Try it yourself: Why exclude internal traffic?

Model answer. Visits from your own staff and testing are not customers; they inflate sessions and distort conversion rates.

Check what you just learned

1. An internal traffic filter removes:
  • All mobile visits
  • Your own team's visits (correct)
  • Revenue
  • Events

Staff visits are not customer behaviour.

2. Personal data such as emails in event parameters:
  • Is fine
  • Improves reports
  • Should not be sent to GA4 (correct)
  • Is required

Keep it out.

Key terms: flip and sort

Recommended event
An event Google has defined names and parameters for.
Custom event
An event you define.
GTM
Google Tag Manager.
Data layer
A structured object the site fills for GTM.
UTM parameter
A tag on a link naming source, medium and campaign.
Channel group
A grouping of traffic based on source and medium.
Consent Mode
Tags adjust behaviour to visitor consent.
keyPoints: Clean data needs internal-traffic filters, referral exclusions, one tag implementation and cross-domain setup.
Consent rules and Consent Mode affect what is measured; keep personal data out of GA4.
Annotate changes that break comparability.

modules.title: Acquisition and engagement analysis
modules.summary: Find where visitors come from, how engaged they are, and what differs by channel, device, country and page, then build the rates that make channels comparable.
modules.outcome: You can read acquisition and engagement reports, build charts of sessions and users by dimension, create calculated rates such as engagement rate and conversion rate, and avoid the traps of averaging rates and adding users.
modules.intro: Once data is flowing, the real work is comparison: which channel brings engaged visitors, which device converts, which page loses people. This module teaches the analysis, using a practice report builder on the traffic of a small learning site. The builder works like GA4's Explorations: you choose dimensions and metrics, filter, and build your own calculated metrics. The numbers are invented, but the patterns (and the mistakes people make reading them) are real.

topics.title: Acquisition: where visits come from
topics.html:
Acquisition reports answer 'where do visitors come from?' GA4 separates two views.

User acquisition and traffic acquisition
User acquisitionTraffic acquisition
Looks atHow a user was first acquiredWhat brought each session
Credit goes toThe first source of the userThe source of that session
Use forWhich channels bring new peopleWhich channels bring visits now

Sessions by channel, and what each is worth

Put Channel on Columns and Sessions on Rows, then sort high to low. Next add Revenue or Users. A big channel is not always a valuable one.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Session ID, User ID, Session Date, Channel, Source / Medium, Device, Country, Landing Page, Engaged, Engagement Seconds, Pageviews, Converted, Revenue.

Reading a channel table
ChannelQuestion to ask
Organic SearchWhich queries and pages bring people? Is it growing?
Paid SearchAre we paying for visitors who then do nothing?
DirectHow much is genuine direct traffic, and how much is untagged?
EmailDo subscribers engage and convert more than average?
Organic SocialIs it brand awareness (many visits, few conversions) or driving action?
ReferralWhich partners send good traffic?
Worked example

Volume is not value

Organic Search brings the most sessions, Email far fewer.

  1. Sessions say who is largest.
  2. Engagement and conversion say who is best: Email visitors engage and buy at higher rates.
  3. Decision: grow the email list, as well as keeping search healthy.

Answer. Rank channels by volume and quality, never volume alone.

Watch out

Source / medium is more detailed than channel. 'Referral' hides which partner; 'Paid Search' hides which campaign. Drill down before concluding, and always say which level you reported.

Common mistakes

  • Ranking channels by sessions only.
  • Ignoring that Direct often hides untagged campaigns.
  • Reporting a channel's share without the time period.
Try it yourself: Why compare engagement and conversion across channels, not just sessions?

Model answer. Sessions show volume only; engagement and conversion show how valuable the visitors are.

Check what you just learned

1. Traffic acquisition credits:
  • The user's first source
  • The country
  • The device
  • The source of each session (correct)

It looks at sessions.

2. A channel with many sessions but few conversions is:
  • Large but low in value (correct)
  • Always the best
  • Broken
  • Direct

Volume is not value.
keyPoints: User acquisition credits the first source of a user; traffic acquisition credits the source of each session.
Rank channels by volume and quality (engagement, conversion, revenue).
Drill from channel to source / medium and campaign.

topics.title: Engagement: what visitors do
topics.html:
Engagement tells you whether visits were meaningful. The key measures:

Engagement measures
MeasureWhat it tells youWatch out
Engaged sessions and engagement rateHow many visits were more than a glanceA landing page that answers the question in 5 seconds can have a low rate and still succeed
Average engagement timeHow long the page or app was in the foregroundPer user or session; skewed by a few long visits
Views (page and screen views) per sessionHow deep visits goMore is not always better: lost visitors browse more
Event count and key eventsWhat they didCheck they are the events you care about
Formula · A calculated rate: engagement rate by channel

Engagement Rate = SUM([Engaged]) / COUNTD([Session ID])

Total engaged sessions divided by total sessions for each mark. In the builder, create it with the Create a calculated field box.

Build an engagement rate

Create Engagement Rate = SUM([Engaged]) / COUNTD([Session ID]), put it on Rows with Channel on Columns, and sort. Which channels hold attention?

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Session ID, User ID, Session Date, Channel, Source / Medium, Device, Country, Landing Page, Engaged, Engagement Seconds, Pageviews, Converted, Revenue.

Worked example

The averages trap

Mobile engagement is 40% on 100 sessions and desktop 80% on 20 sessions.

  1. Average of the two rates: 60%.
  2. Ratio of the totals: (40 + 16) / 120 = 46.7%.
  3. Most sessions are on mobile, so the true overall rate is closer to 40%.

Answer. Always divide total engaged by total sessions. Averaging rates ignores the sizes of the groups.

Watch out

Do not add rates or averages across rows. The overall engagement rate is total engaged sessions over total sessions, not the average of the rows' rates.

Common mistakes

  • Averaging engagement rates across channels.
  • Judging a page by engagement time alone.
  • Comparing engagement rates across very different page types.
Try it yourself: Mobile: 40 engaged of 100 sessions. Desktop: 16 engaged of 20. What is the overall engagement rate?

Model answer. (40 + 16) / (100 + 20) = 56 / 120 = 46.7%.

Check what you just learned

1. Overall engagement rate across groups is:
  • The average of group rates
  • Total engaged sessions ÷ total sessions (correct)
  • The highest rate
  • The median

Add numerators and denominators first.

2. A page that answers a question quickly may show:
  • No sessions
  • Always high engagement
  • A low engagement rate but still succeed (correct)
  • A broken tag

Judge a page by its purpose.
keyPoints: Engagement rate, engagement time, views per session and key events describe what visitors do.
Calculate rates as total over total, not as an average of rates.
Judge a page against its purpose.

topics.title: Audience and technology: device, country, landing page
topics.html:
Breaking traffic down by who and how often explains why numbers differ.

Useful breakdowns
DimensionQuestions it answers
Device categoryDo mobile visitors engage and convert as well as desktop?
Country / cityWhere are visitors, and where do they convert?
New vs returningDo returning visitors convert more?
Landing pageWhich entry pages attract and keep people?
Browser / operating systemIs a bug hurting one browser?

Channel by device: a heat map

Channel down the side, device across the top, colour for Sessions. Switch the colour to Revenue. Where do the sessions and the money differ?

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Session ID, User ID, Session Date, Channel, Source / Medium, Device, Country, Landing Page, Engaged, Engagement Seconds, Pageviews, Converted, Revenue.

Worked example

Mobile traffic that does not convert

Most visits are on mobile, but nearly all purchases are on desktop.

  1. That points to a mobile experience problem (a hard checkout, slow pages) or to people researching on phones and buying later on a computer.
  2. Check mobile page speed and checkout steps, and look at cross-device journeys.
  3. Do not assume the visitors are low quality: the device may be the cause.

Answer. A dimension is a place to look for causes, not a verdict on the visitors.

Watch out

Small groups mislead. A conversion rate of 50% from 4 sessions is not a finding. Show the number of sessions beside every rate, and be cautious with groups under a few dozen.

Common mistakes

  • Concluding from tiny segments.
  • Treating device as the cause without testing.
  • Comparing countries without allowing for audience size.
Try it yourself: What should you show beside a conversion rate for a small segment?

Model answer. The number of sessions it is based on, so readers can judge how reliable it is.

Check what you just learned

1. Which breakdown suggests a mobile experience problem?
  • Country
  • Event name
  • Month
  • Device category (correct)

Compare device rates.

2. A rate from 4 sessions is:
  • Too small to trust (correct)
  • Reliable
  • Perfect
  • Always 100%

Small samples mislead.
keyPoints: Break traffic down by device, location, new versus returning, landing page and browser.
A dimension suggests where to look for causes; test before concluding.
Show the base next to every rate and be careful with small groups.

topics.title: Calculated metrics and building a story
topics.html:
GA4 lets you create calculated metrics (formulas from existing metrics) in Admin, and Explorations let you segment and filter. The idea is the same as the calculated fields you build here: ratios of totals, per-session and per-user measures.

Useful ratios
MeasureFormulaWhat it answers
Engagement rateEngaged sessions ÷ sessionsDo visits matter?
Conversion rate (session key event rate)Sessions with a key event ÷ sessionsDo visits lead to action?
Revenue per sessionRevenue ÷ sessionsWhat is a visit worth?
Average order valueRevenue ÷ purchasesHow big are orders?
Pages per sessionPage views ÷ sessionsHow deep do visits go?

Conversion rate by device

Create Conversion Rate = SUM([Converted]) / COUNTD([Session ID]). Put Device on Columns and the rate on Rows. Then add Sessions to Label so each rate shows its base.

A live chart builder on a table with the fields: Session ID, User ID, Session Date, Channel, Source / Medium, Device, Country, Landing Page, Engaged, Engagement Seconds, Pageviews, Converted, Revenue.

Worked example

A finding written well

Conversion by device.

  1. Headline: Mobile visitors convert far less than desktop, on most of the traffic.
  2. Evidence: mobile is 105 of 160 sessions but 4 of the 16 conversions; desktop is 51 sessions and 10 conversions.
  3. Limit: this is six months of one small site; the tablet group is only 4 sessions.
  4. Action: test a simpler mobile checkout, then compare mobile conversion in a month.

Answer. Lead with the answer, give the numbers with their bases, say what limits it, and propose a test.

Watch out

Correlation is not cause. Mobile visitors converting less does not prove mobile is the problem: perhaps they are at an earlier stage of their decision. Say what you tested and what you did not.

Common mistakes

  • A finding with no base numbers.
  • A recommendation that is not a testable change.
  • Presenting segments of a few sessions as results.
Try it yourself: Write the formula for revenue per session.

Model answer. Total revenue ÷ total sessions (SUM([Revenue]) / COUNTD([Session ID]) in the builder).

Check what you just learned

1. Revenue per session is:
  • Revenue ÷ users
  • Revenue ÷ sessions (correct)
  • Sessions ÷ revenue
  • Revenue × sessions

Total revenue over total sessions.

2. A good recommendation is:
  • Vague
  • A guess
  • A testable change (correct)
  • A colour

Test and measure.

Key terms: flip and sort

User acquisition
Credits a user's first source.
Traffic acquisition
Credits each session's source.
Engagement rate
Engaged sessions ÷ sessions.
Conversion rate
Sessions with a key event ÷ sessions.
Revenue per session
Total revenue ÷ sessions.
Calculated metric
A formula built from existing metrics.
Base
The number of sessions behind a rate.
keyPoints: Calculated metrics are ratios of totals: engagement rate, conversion rate, revenue per session, average order value.
A good finding states the answer, the numbers with their bases, the limits and a test.
Correlation is not cause.

modules.title: Conversions, ecommerce and attribution
modules.summary: Define what a conversion is, track an ecommerce journey as events, build and read funnels, and understand how credit for a conversion is attributed to channels.
modules.outcome: You can choose and name key events, describe the ecommerce events and their parameters, count a funnel with SQL, explain attribution models and their limits, and calculate conversion rate and revenue per channel.
modules.intro: Traffic only matters if it leads somewhere. This module is about the outcomes: what counts as a conversion, how a purchase journey is recorded as events, where people drop out, and which channels deserve credit. The SQL window works on GA4 data in the flat, one-row-per-event form you meet in an export, so you can count a funnel exactly as an analyst would. Google Analytics itself is a cloud service that needs your own website and Google account, so you cannot open it inside this course. What does run here: a practice report builder (dimensions, metrics, calculated metrics, filters and charts, like GA4's Reports and Explorations) on the traffic of a small learning site, and a SQL window on that traffic as it appears in a GA4 export. The lessons describe the real GA4 screens and settings as of this writing; Google changes the interface and some names often, so always check the current help pages.

topics.title: Key events (conversions) and goals
topics.html:
A key event (called a conversion in earlier GA4 documentation and in many tutorials) is an event you mark as important to the business: a purchase, a sign-up, a lead form, a course enrolment. Marking it makes GA4 report it separately and lets you optimise for it, for example in advertising.

Choosing key events
Good key eventWhyWeak choiceWhy not
purchaseRevenue, directlypage_view of the homepageAlmost everyone triggers it
generate_lead on a form submitA qualified enquiryscroll to 90%Interesting, but not an outcome
sign_upStarts a relationshipAny clickToo common to mean anything

Rules of thumb

  • Pick a few key events tied to business goals (one to five), not dozens.
  • Prefer events that happen once per goal (a purchase), and make sure the event fires only on success.
  • Give each a value where possible (price, or an estimated value of a lead).
  • Separate macro conversions (purchase) from micro conversions (viewed pricing, started checkout), and use micro conversions to diagnose, not to celebrate.
  • Check each in DebugView before relying on it.
Formula · Conversion rate

session conversion rate = sessions with a key event ÷ sessions

User conversion rate is users with a key event ÷ users. Say which one you report; they differ when users have several sessions.

Worked example

A key event that fires too often

A thank-you page marked as the conversion can be reloaded or revisited.

  1. Each visit to the page counts a conversion, inflating the number.
  2. Fix: fire a purchase or generate_lead event once, when the action succeeds (and de-duplicate by transaction id).
  3. Compare conversions with orders in the back-end system to check.

Answer. Reconcile key events with a trusted source such as orders or CRM records.

Watch out

Marking everything as a key event destroys its meaning. If every click is a conversion, the conversion rate tells you nothing and optimisation chases the wrong goal.

Common mistakes

  • Counting thank-you page views as conversions.
  • Too many key events.
  • Never reconciling with the order system.
Try it yourself: Which is a better key event for a course site: scroll or purchase?

Model answer. purchase: a direct business outcome, unlike a scroll.

Check what you just learned

1. A good key event is:
  • Any click
  • A scroll
  • A page view of the homepage
  • A direct business outcome such as a purchase (correct)

It reflects a goal.

2. Why reconcile key events with orders?
  • To catch over- or under-counting (correct)
  • It is slower
  • It is required by law
  • To add colour

Back-end records are the check.
keyPoints: Key events (conversions) mark the events that matter to the business; keep them few.
Fire once on success, add a value, and reconcile with the back-end system.
Report conversion rate with a clear denominator (sessions or users).

topics.title: Ecommerce events and parameters
topics.html:
GA4 defines a standard set of ecommerce events that describe a shopping journey. Using exactly these names and parameters unlocks the Monetization reports.

The core ecommerce events
EventFires whenKey parameters
view_item_listA list of products is shownitem_list_name, items
view_itemA product page is vieweditems, value, currency
add_to_cartA product is addeditems, value, currency
begin_checkoutCheckout startsitems, value, currency
add_payment_infoPayment details are enteredpayment_type, value
purchaseThe order is completedtransaction_id, value, currency, items

Getting ecommerce right

  • Send transaction_id so GA4 can ignore a duplicated purchase.
  • Always send currency with value, or revenue will not be reported.
  • Send the items array with ids and names, so product reports work.
  • Fire purchase once, only after payment succeeds.
  • Match the numbers to your orders system: revenue in GA4 should be close, though not identical (refunds, taxes and consent differ).
Worked example

A funnel from events

A learning site's journey.

  1. view_item (course page), add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase.
  2. Counting distinct sessions at each event gives the funnel.
  3. The drop between two steps shows where to look: product page to cart, or checkout to payment.

Answer. The recommended events make a funnel a matter of counting.

Watch out

Missing or wrong currency is the most common reason revenue is blank. Test purchases in DebugView and check value, currency and items arrive.

Common mistakes

  • Firing purchase on page load of the thank-you page, repeated on reload.
  • Revenue sent as text with currency symbols.
  • Different event names from the recommended ones, so Monetization reports stay empty.
Try it yourself: Why send transaction_id with a purchase?

Model answer. So GA4 can recognise and ignore a duplicate of the same order.

Check what you just learned

1. Revenue is missing in reports. First check:
  • The page colour
  • That value and currency are sent with the purchase (correct)
  • The logo
  • The font

Both are needed.

2. transaction_id helps:
  • Speed pages
  • Change fonts
  • De-duplicate purchases (correct)
  • Rename events

It identifies the order.
keyPoints: Use GA4's recommended ecommerce events and parameters: view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase.
Send transaction_id, value, currency and items; fire purchase once, after success.
Reconcile revenue with the orders system.

topics.title: Funnels: counting where people drop out
topics.html:
A funnel counts how many sessions (or users) reach each step of a journey, in order. The drop between steps shows where to focus.

A funnel from flat GA4 events

Distinct sessions that reached each step. Five sessions started; three viewed an item; two added to cart; one began checkout; one purchased.

Tables: ga_events. Starting query:

SELECT event_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
FROM ga_events
WHERE event_name IN ('view_item', 'add_to_cart', 'begin_checkout', 'purchase')
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY sessions DESC;
Reading it
StepSessionsOf the previous step
view_item3n/a
add_to_cart267%
begin_checkout150%
purchase1100%

In GA4 you can build this without SQL in Explore → Funnel exploration, choosing the steps, whether they must happen in order, and whether it is open or closed. The SQL view above is what a BigQuery analyst writes, and it shows exactly what the tool counts: distinct sessions (or users) per step.

Worked example

Which drop matters?

The funnel shows 100 product views, 40 add-to-carts, 20 checkouts, 15 purchases.

  1. Product view to cart: 40% continue.
  2. Cart to checkout: 50% continue.
  3. Checkout to purchase: 75% continue.
  4. The biggest absolute loss is product view to cart (60 people), but the biggest percentage fix may be cart to checkout. Both are worth testing.

Answer. A funnel tells you where, not why. Pair it with session recordings, surveys or a test.

Watch out

Count people or sessions, not events. If a visitor views an item five times, COUNT(*) counts five. Use distinct sessions or users, and decide whether steps must happen in order within one session.

Common mistakes

  • Counting events instead of distinct sessions or users.
  • Ignoring that people skip steps or return later.
  • Treating the funnel as the cause of the drop.
Try it yourself: Which SQL expression counts each session once at a funnel step?

Model answer. COUNT(DISTINCT session_id).

Check what you just learned

1. A funnel step should be counted with:
  • COUNT(*) of events
  • MAX(date)
  • SUM(revenue)
  • COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) (correct)

People or sessions, not events.

2. A funnel shows:
  • Where people drop out (correct)
  • Why people leave
  • Their age
  • Their name

Diagnose the cause separately.
keyPoints: A funnel counts distinct sessions or users reaching each step; the drop shows where to look.
Build it in Explore → Funnel exploration, or with COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in SQL.
A funnel shows where, not why.

topics.title: Attribution: who gets the credit?
topics.html:
A customer might click a search ad, later open an email, and finally return directly to buy. Attribution decides how credit for the conversion is shared among those touchpoints.

Attribution models
ModelHow it gives creditStrengthWeakness
Last clickAll credit to the last touchpoint (often Direct if people return by typing the address)SimpleIgnores everything that built interest
First clickAll credit to the first touchpointShows what introduces peopleIgnores what closes the sale
Data-drivenCredit shared by a model learned from conversion pathsReflects the real contribution of each stepNeeds enough data, less transparent

Attribution in GA4

  • The Advertising section shows conversion paths and compares models.
  • Data-driven attribution is the default for key events, with last click variants available.
  • Attribution lookback windows decide how long before a conversion a touchpoint can earn credit.
  • Different reports (for example traffic acquisition and the attribution reports) can show different numbers because they credit differently.
  • Credit never covers offline influence or visits that GA4 could not link.
Worked example

The same sale, two views

A visitor clicks a paid ad (day 1), opens an email (day 3), and buys by typing the address (day 5).

  1. Last click: Direct gets 100%.
  2. First click: Paid Search gets 100%.
  3. Data-driven: credit is shared across the three, perhaps most to the ad that started the journey.

Answer. No model is 'true'. Choose the one that fits the decision, and know what it hides.

Watch out

Cutting a channel because it 'does not convert' under last click can starve the top of the funnel. Look at assisted contributions and test changes, ideally with an experiment.

Common mistakes

  • Judging channels only by last-click conversions.
  • Comparing numbers from reports that use different attribution.
  • Assuming an attribution model measures cause.
Try it yourself: In the example, which model credits the paid ad fully?

Model answer. First click.

Check what you just learned

1. Last-click attribution gives credit to:
  • The first touchpoint
  • The last touchpoint (correct)
  • All equally
  • None

The final touch gets everything.

2. Data-driven attribution:
  • Ignores data
  • Is always last click
  • Shares credit using a model of conversion paths (correct)
  • Counts events

It learns from paths.

Key terms: flip and sort

Key event
An event marked as important (formerly conversion).
Ecommerce event
A recommended event in a shopping journey.
transaction_id
Identifies an order so duplicates are ignored.
Funnel
Counts of sessions reaching each step.
Attribution
Sharing credit among touchpoints.
Last click
All credit to the final touchpoint.
Lookback window
How far back a touchpoint can earn credit.
keyPoints: Attribution shares credit among touchpoints: last click, first click, data-driven.
Different reports can credit differently; lookback windows matter.
No model proves cause: use experiments for decisions that matter.

modules.title: Explorations, audiences and the BigQuery export
modules.summary: Go beyond standard reports with explorations, segments and audiences, and learn what a GA4 export looks like and how to analyse it with SQL.
modules.outcome: You can choose the right exploration type, build segments and audiences, explain returning users and retention, and write SQL on flat GA4 event data to find abandoners and returning users.
modules.intro: Standard reports answer common questions. Real analysis soon needs more: a funnel you define yourself, the people who added to cart but never bought, the visitors who return within a week. GA4 gives you Explorations, segments and audiences for that, and, for the full detail, an export to BigQuery where every event is a row you can query with SQL. This module covers both, and the SQL runs here on a flattened version of that data. Google Analytics itself is a cloud service that needs your own website and Google account, so you cannot open it inside this course. What does run here: a practice report builder (dimensions, metrics, calculated metrics, filters and charts, like GA4's Reports and Explorations) on the traffic of a small learning site, and a SQL window on that traffic as it appears in a GA4 export. The lessons describe the real GA4 screens and settings as of this writing; Google changes the interface and some names often, so always check the current help pages.

topics.title: Explorations: the analysis types
topics.html:
Explorations (in Explore) let you build your own analyses from the same data as the standard reports. The main techniques:

Exploration techniques
TechniqueAnswersExample
Free formAny table or chart of dimensions and metricsSessions and revenue by channel and device
Funnel explorationHow many people complete each step, and where they dropView item to purchase
Path explorationWhat people do before or after an eventWhat pages do people visit after the pricing page?
Segment overlapHow segments overlapMobile users who are also returning users
Cohort explorationHow groups who started together behave over timeRetention of users by the week they first visited
User explorerThe journey of individual (anonymous) usersWhy this user never completed checkout
User lifetimeValue of users over their lifeRevenue per user over their first 90 days

Working well in explorations

  • Start from a question, not from the available buttons.
  • Choose dimensions and metrics deliberately, and apply filters and segments to narrow.
  • Mind sampling and thresholds: explorations can be sampled on large data, and thresholds can hide small groups.
  • Save useful explorations and share them with your team.
  • Check results against a standard report: they should agree where they measure the same thing.
Worked example

Choosing the exploration

'Where do visitors go after the pricing page, and do they come back?'

  1. 'Where do they go next?': a path exploration starting at the pricing page.
  2. 'Do they come back?': a cohort exploration of users who viewed pricing.
  3. Different questions use different techniques.

Answer. Match the technique to the shape of the question.

Watch out

Explorations are limited by data retention settings for user-level data: if retention is two months, you cannot explore events older than that at user level, though standard reports remain. Choose retention deliberately.

Common mistakes

  • Building a complicated table when a standard report answers it.
  • Not checking sampling or thresholds.
  • Forgetting data retention limits.
Try it yourself: Which technique shows how a group of users behaves over the weeks after they first visit?

Model answer. A cohort exploration.

Check what you just learned

1. A funnel exploration shows:
  • Passwords
  • Server settings
  • Page colours
  • Where people drop out between steps (correct)

Step-by-step completion.

2. Retention settings affect:
  • How far back user-level explorations can go (correct)
  • Standard reports only
  • Page speed
  • Colours

Choose retention deliberately.
keyPoints: Free form, funnel, path, segment overlap, cohort, user explorer and user lifetime cover most custom analyses.
Start from a question, apply segments and filters, and mind sampling and thresholds.
Data retention limits what can be explored at user level.

topics.title: Segments, audiences and retargeting
topics.html:
A segment is a subset of your data defined by conditions (users who purchased, sessions from mobile). An audience is a segment that GA4 keeps updating and can send to Google Ads or other products, for example to show a reminder ad to people who added to cart and did not buy.

Segments and audiences
SegmentAudience
Used forAnalysis in explorationsMarketing and personalisation, and also analysis
UpdatesApplied to the data you viewContinuously, as people qualify
ExampleUsers who viewed pricing at least twicePeople who added to cart in the last 7 days and did not purchase

Who added to cart but never purchased?

Users with an add_to_cart event, minus users with a purchase. This is exactly what a 'cart abandoners' audience contains. EXCEPT subtracts the second list from the first.

Tables: ga_events. Starting query:

SELECT DISTINCT user_pseudo_id
FROM ga_events
WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart'
EXCEPT
SELECT user_pseudo_id
FROM ga_events
WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
ORDER BY 1;

Audience design

  • Define the goal first: who do you want to reach, and with what message?
  • Use conditions with time windows ('in the last 7 days'), so the audience stays relevant.
  • Mind minimum audience sizes that advertising platforms require.
  • Respect consent: audiences for advertising rely on consented users, and some people cannot be included.
  • Exclude people who already converted.
Worked example

A good abandoner audience

A shop wants to remind people who left without buying.

  1. Include: add_to_cart in the last 7 days.
  2. Exclude: purchase in the last 7 days.
  3. Message: a gentle reminder, not a barrage.

Answer. The audience is the SQL idea in the example, kept up to date and linked to ads.

Watch out

Remarketing is regulated in many places, and people find it intrusive when it follows them everywhere. Use consent, frequency caps and exclusions, and follow the platform's policies.

Common mistakes

  • Audiences with no exclusions, so buyers keep seeing reminders.
  • Windows that are too long, so the message is stale.
  • Ignoring consent and policy rules.
Try it yourself: What should a cart abandoner audience exclude?

Model answer. People who have already purchased.

Check what you just learned

1. An audience differs from a segment because it:
  • Cannot be used
  • Is kept up to date and can be exported to advertising (correct)
  • Has no conditions
  • Is slower

It is a live group you can reach.

2. A cart-abandoner audience should exclude:
  • Visitors
  • Mobile users
  • Purchasers (correct)
  • Everyone

They already bought.
keyPoints: A segment is for analysis; an audience is kept up to date and can be sent to advertising products.
Define the goal, use time windows, add exclusions and respect consent.
EXCEPT in SQL is the same idea as 'did A but not B'.

topics.title: The BigQuery export and SQL on GA4 data
topics.html:
GA4 can export its raw event data to BigQuery, Google's data warehouse. There each event is a row, so you can answer questions standard reports cannot, join GA4 to other data, and avoid sampling. Export has daily and streaming options with limits that Google changes, so check the current documentation.

What the export looks like
Column (simplified)Meaning
event_dateThe date of the event
event_nameThe event, such as purchase
user_pseudo_idA pseudonymous identifier for the browser or device
event_paramsA repeated field of parameters (name and value) for the event
traffic_sourceHow the user was first acquired
device, geoDevice and location details
itemsThe products in ecommerce events

The practice window here uses a flattened version: one row per event with the common fields as plain columns. The reasoning is identical; only the access to nested fields (UNNEST) differs. Everything you learned in the SQL courses applies: filter, group, COUNT DISTINCT, joins and window functions.

New and returning users

Sessions per user: users with two or more sessions are returning users. Change the query to count them.

Tables: ga_events. Starting query:

SELECT user_pseudo_id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
FROM ga_events
GROUP BY user_pseudo_id
ORDER BY sessions DESC, user_pseudo_id;
Worked example

Why analysts use the export

A question the interface cannot answer: 'What share of purchasers viewed our pricing page first?'

  1. In BigQuery, find sessions with a page_view of the pricing page before a purchase.
  2. Count distinct purchasing sessions with and without it.
  3. The result needs no sampling and can join to a customer table.

Answer. The export turns GA4 into a normal analytics database.

Watch out

Remember cost and privacy: BigQuery charges for data scanned, so filter by _TABLE_SUFFIX date and select only the columns you need; and the export holds pseudonymous identifiers, which are still personal data under many laws.

Common mistakes

  • Scanning every table with no date filter.
  • Forgetting UNNEST for parameters.
  • Treating user_pseudo_id as a real person's id.
Try it yourself: Why filter by date when querying the export tables?

Model answer. BigQuery charges by data scanned, so a date filter reads fewer tables and costs less.

Check what you just learned

1. In the export, each row is:
  • A report
  • A chart
  • A user's name
  • An event (correct)

Event-level data.

2. Why filter by date in BigQuery?
  • To reduce data scanned and cost (correct)
  • Required by law
  • To add colour
  • It is faster to type

You pay for what you scan.
keyPoints: The BigQuery export gives one row per event, unsampled, for SQL analysis.
Parameters live in nested fields that need UNNEST; this course practises on a flattened version.
Filter dates and select columns to control cost, and handle pseudonymous ids as personal data.

topics.title: Retention, cohorts and predictive metrics
topics.html:
Retention measures whether people come back. A cohort is a group who started at the same time (users who first visited in the same week); a retention table shows what share of each cohort is active one week later, two weeks later, and so on. GA4's Retention report and cohort exploration show this.

Retention questions
QuestionWhere to look
Do new users return?Retention report: new vs returning, and the retention curve
Do users who did X come back more?Cohort exploration with a segment
How valuable is a user over time?User lifetime exploration

GA4 can also calculate predictive metrics (such as purchase probability and churn probability) using machine learning, when your property has enough data and meets eligibility conditions. These can power predictive audiences, for example 'people likely to purchase in the next 7 days'.

Worked example

Retention changes the question

A campaign brings 1,000 new users, 600 of them in the first week.

  1. Acquisition says it worked: many visits.
  2. Retention shows only 5% return in week two, against 20% for organic users.
  3. The campaign buys visits, not relationships, so judge it on value over time.

Answer. Short-term traffic can hide long-term weakness; retention reveals it.

Watch out

Predictive metrics need volume and recent conversions to be available, and they are probabilities, not promises. Test an audience before betting a budget on it.

Common mistakes

  • Judging a campaign only on first-visit traffic.
  • Reading predictive audiences as certainties.
  • Comparing cohorts of different sizes without showing the base.
Try it yourself: What is a cohort?

Model answer. A group of users who started at the same time (for example first visited in the same week), followed over time.

Check what you just learned

1. A cohort is:
  • A report colour
  • A group of users who started together (correct)
  • A page
  • A tag

Followed over time.

2. Retention can show that a campaign:
  • Is free
  • Has no visits
  • Brought visits but few returning users (correct)
  • Is illegal

Volume is not loyalty.

Key terms: flip and sort

Exploration
A custom analysis in GA4's Explore area.
Segment
A subset of data defined by conditions.
Audience
A segment kept up to date and exportable.
BigQuery export
Raw GA4 events in a data warehouse.
Cohort
A group that started together.
Retention
The share of a cohort that returns.
Predictive metric
A machine-learning estimate such as purchase probability.
keyPoints: Retention shows whether groups come back; cohorts group users by start time.
Retention can reverse the verdict on a campaign that looked successful.
Predictive metrics need data and are probabilities.

modules.title: Measurement strategy, reporting and privacy
modules.summary: Plan measurement from business goals, report to decision makers, understand the limits of analytics data, and handle privacy responsibly.
modules.outcome: You can turn goals into KPIs and events in a measurement plan, build a dashboard that leads to action, explain sampling, thresholds and attribution limits, and describe responsible, consent-aware practice.
modules.intro: The best analytics setup starts not with the tool but with a plan: what decisions need support, which measures show progress, and which events deliver them. It ends with reporting people act on, an honest account of what the data cannot tell you, and respect for the privacy of the people behind the numbers. This module ties the course together and leads into the final project, where you analyse the traffic of the learning site and write the measurement plan and findings. Google Analytics itself is a cloud service that needs your own website and Google account, so you cannot open it inside this course. What does run here: a practice report builder (dimensions, metrics, calculated metrics, filters and charts, like GA4's Reports and Explorations) on the traffic of a small learning site, and a SQL window on that traffic as it appears in a GA4 export. The lessons describe the real GA4 screens and settings as of this writing; Google changes the interface and some names often, so always check the current help pages.

topics.title: A measurement plan: from goals to events
topics.html:
A measurement plan is a short document that links business goals to the numbers and events that will show progress. It stops you collecting data nobody uses and missing data everyone needs.

Goal to event
Business goalKPIEvents and parameters neededSegments to compare
Grow course salesPurchases, conversion rate, revenueview_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase with value, currency, itemsChannel, device, new vs returning
Build an email listSign-ups per 1,000 sessionssign_up (with method)Landing page, channel
Help learners succeedShare who finish a first lessonA custom lesson_complete event with lesson_idCourse, country
Make marketing efficientCost per purchase, revenue per session by channelCampaign tags, cost data importedSource / medium, campaign

What a good measurement plan contains

  • Business goals and the decisions they support.
  • KPIs with exact definitions (the numerator, the denominator, the period).
  • Events and parameters, named and documented, with who owns each.
  • Dimensions and segments to compare.
  • Targets or benchmarks, so a number can be judged.
  • Data quality and privacy notes: consent, personal data, retention.
  • Reporting: who sees which report, how often.
Worked example

A KPI defined exactly

'Conversion rate' as the team means it.

  1. Numerator: sessions with a purchase event.
  2. Denominator: all sessions, excluding internal traffic.
  3. Period: calendar month, by default channel group.
  4. Written down once, so every report gives the same number.

Answer. An unwritten definition is where disagreements about numbers begin.

Watch out

Tracking everything 'just in case' costs effort and creates risk (privacy, noise). Track what a decision needs, and add more when a question arises.

Common mistakes

  • KPIs without definitions.
  • Events nobody can explain.
  • No targets, so numbers cannot be judged.
Try it yourself: Write the definition of 'session conversion rate' in one sentence.

Model answer. Sessions with a purchase event divided by all sessions (excluding internal traffic), for the chosen period.

Check what you just learned

1. A measurement plan starts from:
  • Tags
  • A tool
  • Colours
  • Business goals and the decisions they support (correct)

Goals first.

2. A well-defined KPI states:
  • Numerator, denominator and period (correct)
  • Only its name
  • A colour
  • A logo

Exactness prevents disputes.
keyPoints: A measurement plan links goals, KPIs, events, segments and targets.
Define each KPI exactly: numerator, denominator and period.
Track what decisions need, and document it.

topics.title: Dashboards and reporting that drive action
topics.html:
Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio) is Google's free tool for turning GA4 and other data into shareable dashboards. Whatever the tool, the principles of good reporting are the same as in the visualisation courses.

Principles of a useful report

  • Audience first: executives want a few KPIs and the story; analysts want to explore.
  • Lead with the answer: a headline number against a target or last period.
  • Few, well-chosen metrics: five to seven on a page.
  • Compare: every number needs a comparison (previous period, target, same period last year).
  • Explain: a sentence of insight beside the chart, and a recommended action.
  • Consistency: the same definitions as the measurement plan.
  • Refresh and ownership: who maintains it, how often it updates.
Report types
ReportAudienceContent
Executive summaryLeadershipTop KPIs vs targets, three insights, one decision to make
Channel performanceMarketingSessions, engagement, conversion and revenue by channel, with trends
Funnel and site healthProduct and UXFunnel steps, device split, page issues
Ad hoc analysisAnalystsExplorations and SQL for a specific question
Worked example

A one-page monthly report

For the marketing lead of the learning site.

  1. Top row: sessions, engagement rate, conversion rate, revenue, each against last month.
  2. A bar chart of conversion rate by channel with sessions shown.
  3. A short note: 'Email converts at 26% on 19 sessions; paid search had no purchases on 31 sessions. Action: review paid targeting.'
  4. A footnote with definitions and the data range.

Answer. Numbers, comparison, insight, action, definitions: the five parts of a report people use.

Watch out

Beware data thresholds, sampling and 'cardinality' limits: reports can hide small groups, explorations can be sampled, and dimensions with very many values can be grouped into '(other)'. Check the data-quality icon and note the limitation in your report.

Common mistakes

  • A dashboard of twenty charts and no insight.
  • Numbers with no comparison.
  • Different definitions in different reports.
Try it yourself: What five things does a useful report contain?

Model answer. Key numbers, a comparison, an insight, a recommended action and the definitions.

Check what you just learned

1. Every number in a report needs:
  • A decoration
  • A comparison such as a target or last period (correct)
  • A long name
  • A logo

A number alone has no meaning.

2. Executives usually want:
  • Twenty charts
  • Raw events
  • A few KPIs and the story (correct)
  • Code

Short and decision-focused.
keyPoints: Report for the audience: lead with the answer, compare, explain and recommend.
Use the same definitions as the measurement plan.
Note sampling, thresholds and other limits.

topics.title: Data limits, privacy and responsible analytics
topics.html:
Good analysts know what their data cannot tell them, and treat the people behind it with respect.

Limits to remember
LimitWhat it means
Consent and ad blockersSome visitors are not measured, so reports undercount
SamplingLarge explorations may be based on a sample; standard reports are not sampled in the same way
ThresholdsSmall groups can be hidden to protect privacy
CardinalityDimensions with very many values are grouped as '(other)'
Modelled dataGA4 can estimate some behaviour of non-consenting users; estimates are not exact
Cross-device gapsOne person on a phone and a laptop may look like two users
Attribution gapsOffline and untracked influence is invisible
Not causalReports show association, not proof of cause

Responsible practice

  • Minimise: collect what you need; do not send personal data to GA4.
  • Be transparent: a clear privacy notice and consent choices.
  • Respect choices: honour declined consent; do not work around it.
  • Limit retention and access; remove people who no longer need it.
  • Check the law for your visitors: for example the EU's GDPR and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; your privacy or legal team decides what applies.
  • Do not re-identify people: combining pseudonymous data with other data to identify individuals can break the rules and trust.
Worked example

A sensible limit statement

A report on conversion by country.

  1. 'UAE shows 3 conversions from 12 sessions; treat as indicative only.'
  2. 'Figures cover consenting visitors; true traffic is higher.'
  3. 'Data is from GA4 and may differ from the payment system by a few percent.'

Answer. Naming the limits makes a report more trustworthy, not less.

Watch out

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Privacy law is changing and varies by country, so involve the people responsible for it in your organisation.

Common mistakes

  • Presenting estimates as exact.
  • Collecting personal data 'to be safe'.
  • Trying to identify individual visitors from analytics data.
Try it yourself: Why might GA4 undercount visitors?

Model answer. Visitors who decline consent or use ad blockers are not measured in the usual way.

Check what you just learned

1. Sampling means:
  • All data is used
  • Data is encrypted
  • Data is deleted
  • A subset of data is used for a large query (correct)

Results are estimates from a sample.

2. Responsible analytics includes:
  • Minimising data and respecting consent (correct)
  • Collecting every personal detail
  • Re-identifying visitors
  • Ignoring the law

Respect people's choices.

Key terms: flip and sort

Measurement plan
Links goals, KPIs, events and segments.
KPI
A measure tied to a goal, with a definition.
Looker Studio
Google's free dashboard tool.
Sampling
Using a subset of data for a large query.
Threshold
Hiding small groups to protect privacy.
Consent
A visitor's permission for tracking.
Pseudonymous id
An identifier that is not a name but is still personal data.
keyPoints: Reports undercount and estimate: consent, ad blockers, sampling, thresholds, cardinality, cross-device gaps and attribution gaps.
Minimise data, respect consent, limit retention, and do not re-identify people.
State limits plainly; involve privacy and legal teams.
